issue.issue_text: Whether the Special Court constituted under the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002 has the jurisdiction to try the scheduled offence connected to the offence of money-laundering.

facts: The case involved a challenge to a summoning order based on the argument that the Special Court lacked territorial jurisdiction.

The core legal question was whether a Special Court constituted under the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA) could try the underlying 'scheduled offence' in addition to the offence of money-laundering itself.

law.description: This section mandates that an offence of money-laundering and any connected scheduled offence shall be triable by the Special Court constituted for the area in which the offence of money-laundering has been committed.

This section provides a procedure for when a court other than the PMLA Special Court has already taken cognizance of the scheduled offence. It states that upon an application by the authorized authority, that other court shall commit (transfer) the case relating to the scheduled offence to the Special Court that is handling the money-laundering case.
This section gives the PMLA an overriding effect over any other law that may be inconsistent with it.

application: The Court conducted a combined reading of clauses (a) and (c) of Section 44(1) of the PMLA.
The Court determined that these clauses give 'primacy' to the Special Court constituted under the PMLA.
It established a clear rule: the jurisdiction for the trial of the scheduled offence follows the jurisdiction for the trial of the money-laundering offence, not the other way around.

The Court explained that Section 44(1)(a) makes it 'crystal clear' that the Special Court where the money-laundering offence was committed is empowered to try both the money-laundering offence and the connected scheduled offence.

Furthermore, the Court clarified that even if another court has already started proceedings for the scheduled offence, Section 44(1)(c) creates a mandatory obligation for that court to transfer the case to the PMLA Special Court upon receiving an application.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the Special Court constituted under the PMLA does have the jurisdiction to try the scheduled offence connected to the offence of money-laundering. The statutory scheme of Section 44 ensures that both offences are tried together by the same Special Court, specifically the one that has jurisdiction over the money-laundering offence.

issue.issue_text: Whether the issue of territorial jurisdiction can be decided in a writ petition, especially when there is a serious factual dispute about the place of commission of the offence.

facts: The petitioner filed a writ petition in the Supreme Court challenging the territorial jurisdiction of a Special Court in Ghaziabad.
The case involved alleged offences related to online crowdfunding, where the acquisition of the 'proceeds of crime' took place in the virtual world.

This created a serious factual dispute about the specific physical location(s) where the offence was committed, specifically where the proceeds of the crime were concealed, possessed, acquired, or used.
law: The Court referred to its previous decision in *Kaushik Chatterjee vs. State of Haryana & Ors.*
The key legal principle established in that case is that the issue of territorial jurisdiction in criminal cases depends on facts that must be established through evidence.

Territorial jurisdiction is determined by various factors outlined in the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.), such as the place where the offence was committed, where its consequences ensued, or where the property involved was found.
application: The Court applied the principle that jurisdiction is a fact-based inquiry.

It reasoned that determining which court has jurisdiction in this specific case requires a factual investigation into where the alleged proceeds of crime were handled (concealed, possessed, acquired, or used).
The Court held that a writ petition is not the proper forum for such a detailed factual inquiry, as it would require the presentation and evaluation of evidence.
This process of evidence-taking is the function of a Trial Court, not a court exercising writ jurisdiction.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the issue of territorial jurisdiction cannot be decided in a writ petition, especially when it involves a serious factual dispute about where the offence occurred. The Court dismissed the writ petition, stating that this question must be raised before the Trial Court (the Special Court), as its resolution depends on the evidence that unfolds during the trial.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the issue of territorial jurisdiction can be decided in a writ petition, especially when there is a serious factual dispute about the place of commission of the offence.
appellant_arguments: No part of the alleged offence of money-laundering occurred within the jurisdiction of the Special Court in Ghaziabad.
The petitioner's bank account, where the alleged proceeds of crime were deposited, is located in Navi Mumbai, Maharashtra.
The proceedings for the provisional attachment of the bank account were initiated in New Delhi.
Lodging the complaint in Ghaziabad is an abuse of the court's process and is vitiated because it was done at the instance of the founder of the Hindu IT Cell.
The Special Judge should have returned the complaint under Section 201 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
The order taking cognizance is vitiated by non-application of mind.

cases.case_name: Kaushik Chatterjee v. State of Haryana & Ors.
cases.principle: The issue of territorial jurisdiction cannot be decided in a writ petition, especially when there is a serious factual dispute about the place or places of commission of the offence. This question should be raised before the trial court as the answer depends on evidence.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The offence of money-laundering must be tried only by the Special Court designated for such offences within the jurisdiction where the offence of money-laundering was committed.
obiter: The issue of a court's jurisdiction to try an offence or offender, including territorial jurisdiction, is dependent upon facts that must be established through evidence.
Issues of territorial jurisdiction are to be decided in accordance with the rules set forth in Sections 177 to 184 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
Ordinarily, every offence should be inquired into and tried by a court within whose local jurisdiction it was committed.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court concluded that the issue of territorial jurisdiction cannot be decided in a writ petition, particularly when there is a serious factual dispute regarding the place or places where the offence was committed. Answering the question of jurisdiction in a money-laundering case requires a factual inquiry and evidence to determine where any of the processes or activities mentioned in Section 3 of the PMLA—such as concealment, possession, acquisition, or use of proceeds of crime—were carried out. Therefore, this question must be raised before the Trial Court, which is the proper forum to adjudicate such factual disputes.
legal_tests_applied: The issue of jurisdiction of a court to try an “offence” or “offender” as well as the issue of territorial jurisdiction, depend upon facts established through evidence.

Determining territorial jurisdiction in a PMLA case requires a factual enquiry into the place where the alleged proceeds of crime were (i) concealed; or (ii) possessed; or (iii) acquired; or (iv) used.
why_appellant_lost: The court held that a writ petition is not the appropriate forum to decide the issue of territorial jurisdiction when it involves a serious factual dispute about the place of commission of the offence.
The determination of territorial jurisdiction in this case is not a pure question of law but depends on evidence that has yet to be presented and evaluated.
The question of where the processes or activities of money-laundering under Section 3 occurred is a question of fact that can only be answered by the Trial Court after evidence unfolds.
why_respondent_won: The court affirmed the principle that jurisdictional questions dependent on facts must be raised before the trial court, which is bound to consider them.

The court agreed that an answer to the jurisdictional challenge would depend upon evidence as to the places where any one or more of the processes or activities mentioned in Section 3 were carried out, which is a matter for trial.
policy_considerations: The decision reinforces the procedural propriety and established judicial hierarchy where trial courts are the designated forum for resolving factual disputes, while writ courts are generally not equipped for or intended to conduct such inquiries.
